lives_at.note: NOT LINKED ON PURPOSE. The Clybourne place is several miles up the North Branch, around the ground of the later North Chicago Rolling Mills, and data/structures/clybourn_cabins.json declares itself displaced from that position. Pointing a household at a building the dataset says is in the wrong place would launder a known error into a residence claim.

persons.name: Archibald Clybourne

occupation.note: 'Archibald Clybourne, butcher, came in 1823, then living north of the town limits, and not a voter in the new village.' An earlier list Andreas prints has, under 'Butchers - Archibald Clybourne', the North Branch; he butchered for the garrison.

persons.note: DOCUMENTED AND DELIBERATELY OUTSIDE THE TOWN, which is why this household's division is 'outside_town' and why it matters. Andreas's own roster explains the status in the same clause that gives the trade: he lived north of the limits and could not vote in the village. 'Julia K. Clark, half-brother of A. Clybourne, then living with him' is named in the next clause and is written into this household. The Clybourne family had been at Chicago since the 1820s and its assessment appears in the Peoria County taxpayer lists of 1825. THE TOWN'S OWN ROLLS, 1833-1835 — CORROBORATION, NOT A GRADE. The early Chicago voter and tax lists held by the Illinois Regional Archives Depository name this person 1 time: Tax list of the Town of Chicago, 1833 — “Clybourne, Archibald” (tax_1833_019, line 71). These are the town's own contemporary paper rather than a recollection of it, and each appearance says that a man of that name stood on that roll in that year — no more. The reading is twice mediated (Schulz's transcription, then Genealogy Trails' republication) and this project has not seen the IRAD originals. Under the ratified ladder (T-0513) the 1835 poll with a second independent source is attested, the 1835 poll alone or a 1833/1834 list with another source is inferred, and a single appearance with nothing else is a projected resident. This pass WRITES THE EVIDENCE AND MOVES NO GRADE — T-0515 applies the ladder against every source at once. Identity by the crosswalk's own rule: one resident of the surname 'Clybourne' agrees with the entry's forenames; 1 bearer(s) of the surname were considered. (data/research/civic/voter_crosswalk.json). THE FEDERAL TRACT SALES — A TRANSACTION, NOT A RESIDENCE. The Illinois State Archives' Public Domain Land Tract Sales database records this name entering federal ground around the town: “CLYBOURNE ARCHIBALD” — 2 sales between 1833-10-22 and 1833-10-24, T39N R14E sec 16 (ls0137, ls0138). A sale is a TRANSACTION and never a residence — the register's Residence column reads 'UNKNOWN' here, so it says a man of this name was buying land in these years and nothing about where he lived or what stood on the ground. The reading is transcription-mediated; the adjudication is data/research/land_sales/resident_crosswalk.json. This pass WRITES THE EVIDENCE AND MOVES NO GRADE — under the ratified ladder (T-0513) the grade is applied by T-0515 against every source at once, and a purchase corroborates rather than mints.

research_note: THE BUTCHER WHO LIVED OUTSIDE THE CORPORATION, and the household that forces the schema's division field to have a value for people the town did not count. Chicago's population figures - 350 in 1833, 3,265 in the town census of 1835 - are figures for a corporate area with a boundary that moved twice in eighteen months, and households like this one fall outside it while supplying it with meat. ANY LATER COUNT MUST DECIDE WHETHER TO INCLUDE THEM and this field is where that decision gets made. THE FAMILY'S BUILDINGS ARE A KNOWN PROBLEM IN THIS DATASET: data/structures/clybourn_cabins.json says outright that it is DISPLACED - the attested ground is several miles up the North Branch, outside the modelled box - so lives_at is left null here rather than pointing at a record that admits it is in the wrong place.
